cards.front: List 2 physical factors ignored in the standard particle model of a projectile.

options.explanation: The standard particle model treats the projectile as a point mass and neglects air resistance, so these two physical factors are ignored.

Gravity is included as the projectile’s constant downward acceleration, while mass is not usually needed once the forces are modelled. The ignored factors are air resistance and the object’s dimensions.
Initial speed and launch angle are essential starting conditions for the motion, not assumptions omitted by the model. The model ignores air resistance and the dimensions of the object.
The velocity components describe the projectile’s motion and are used in the equations. The particle model instead ignores air resistance and the physical dimensions of the object.

cards.front: Why is the horizontal acceleration of a projectile modeled as zero?
cards.back: There are no horizontal forces acting on the particle after launch.

options.text: There are no horizontal forces acting on the particle after launch.
options.explanation: With no horizontal force after launch, Newton’s second law gives zero horizontal acceleration, so the horizontal velocity remains constant throughout the flight.

options.text: There are no vertical forces acting on the particle after launch.
options.explanation: Gravity is a vertical force and causes the projectile’s downward acceleration. The horizontal acceleration is zero because there are no horizontal forces acting after launch.

options.text: The particle has no velocity acting on it after launch.
options.explanation: A projectile continues moving with its initial velocity components after launch. Its horizontal acceleration is zero specifically because no horizontal force acts, not because its velocity disappears.

options.text: The particle has constant vertical velocity after launch.
options.explanation: The vertical velocity changes because gravity produces constant downward acceleration. The horizontal velocity is constant because no horizontal force acts on the particle.

cards.front: A particle is launched with speed $U$ at angle $\theta$ to the horizontal. What is its initial vertical velocity component $u_y$?

options.explanation: Resolving the initial velocity vector vertically gives the opposite component in the right-angled triangle, so the initial vertical velocity is $U\sin\theta$.
Using cosine gives the component adjacent to the launch angle, which is horizontal. The vertical component is opposite the angle and therefore uses sine: $U\sin\theta$.
Dividing by sine is not the rule for resolving this velocity vector and gives the wrong dependence on the angle. The vertical component is found by multiplying $U$ by $\sin\theta$.
Tangent relates the two velocity components rather than directly resolving the speed into the vertical component. The correct vertical component is $U\sin\theta$.

cards.front: A particle is launched with speed $U$ at angle $\theta$ to the horizontal. What is its initial horizontal velocity component $u_x$?

options.explanation: Resolving the initial velocity vector horizontally gives the component adjacent to the launch angle, so the initial horizontal velocity is $U\cos\theta$.
Sine gives the component opposite the launch angle, which is vertical. The horizontal component is adjacent to the angle and is therefore $U\cos\theta$.
Dividing by cosine is not the rule for resolving the velocity and produces an incorrect value. The horizontal component is obtained by multiplying $U$ by $\cos\theta$.
Tangent gives the ratio of the vertical component to the horizontal component, not the horizontal component directly. Resolving the speed horizontally gives $U\cos\theta$.

cards.front: Which variable links the horizontal and vertical SUVAT equations in a projectile problem?

options.explanation: The same elapsed time $t$ describes both the horizontal and vertical motion, allowing the two independent SUVAT equations to be connected in a projectile problem.
Horizontal and vertical distances generally differ, so distance does not directly link the two equations. The common variable is the elapsed time $t$ since launch.
The horizontal and vertical accelerations are different: horizontal acceleration is zero while vertical acceleration is $-g$. The variable shared by both equations is time $t$.
The horizontal and vertical velocity components are generally different, so velocity is not the single linking variable. Both equations use the same elapsed time $t$.
